entries.test: Public moderation records and studies of Facebook's AI-generated content would show whether lax enforcement enabled its widespread proliferation.
entries.note: The claim concerns both prevalence and its cause.

entries.test: Public training-data disclosures, licensing records and AI product outputs would show whether companies commercially reproduce user-created content taken without permission.
entries.note: The concrete allegation is unauthorized appropriation and resale; 'stealing' also conveys moral condemnation.
The normalization removes 'what appears to be' from the claim about the rest of the internet. The universal Common Crawl assertion is separately checkable.
The proposition includes companies' private hopes about replacing humans.

entries.test: The New York Times complaint, its exhibits and public training-data evidence would show whether they establish substantial use of Times content in GPT-4 and other models.
entries.note: 'I'd argue' introduces an asserted conclusion, rather than a probability estimate.
Here 'stealing' is his moral characterization of training on others' works, without a specified legal standard.

entries.test: Published descriptions of LLM training and controlled tests of copying versus generalization would establish whether models operate as the described plagiarism mechanism.
entries.note: The passage makes a concrete technical assertion despite its polemical wording.
Calling LLMs theft expresses a moral judgment. The embedded OpenAI quotation is a separate factual assertion.
The central commitment labels LLM development theft rather than specifying a legal violation.
The explanation rests on an exclusive attribution of private motives to product makers.
'Effectively a subsidiary' supplies no agreed threshold of control, and the added thief characterization is evaluative.
The passage addresses the tech industry generally; the normalization narrows it to generative AI. 'Useful' and repeating unspecified mistakes supply no shared test.
The extracted proposition centers on his assessment of output as mediocre.
He judges use cases emailed to him, not all proposed use cases. 'Contrived' versus useful is his evaluative distinction.
This recommends skepticism.

entries.test: Public demonstrations and evaluations of AI systems available at publication would show whether they could collaboratively clarify software requirements and discuss implementation.
entries.note: Although prompted by Devin, the wording makes a claim about AI generally.

entries.test: The demonstrated task's requirements, generated code, execution record and comparable human completion times would test the stated shortcomings.
entries.note: The normalization is supported by the remainder of the paragraph, although the selected quotation alone is evaluative.
This is a sarcastic put-down, not a specified comparative assessment.

entries.test: Public evidence of financial collapse at several referenced tech companies, attributable to their generative AI activities, would establish the predicted ruin.
entries.note: 'I believe ... is going to' expresses a firm prediction without a deadline.

entries.test: Public estimates of usable training-data stocks and model developers' data consumption at publication would show whether available new data was approaching exhaustion.
entries.note: The plain reading concerns usable training data, not every possible sequence of text.

entries.test: Public court judgments, settlements or enforcement actions following disclosure of training-data acquisition would show whether the search for more data brought significant legal consequences.
entries.note: The forecast depends on disclosure and supplies no deadline.

entries.test: Public training disclosures and model evaluations would show whether data scarcity led companies to ingest synthetic content and thereby destroy their models' ability to answer usefully.
entries.note: The forecast asserts destructive collapse, not merely some synthetic-data use.

entries.test: Public Firefly training disclosures and Adobe Stock provenance records would show whether Firefly accidentally ingested AI-generated stock images by publication.
entries.note: The normalization drops the explicit assertion that Firefly's ingestion was accidental.

entries.test: Public hallucination research and reliability evaluations in mission-critical applications would test whether hallucinations resist practical solutions and preclude every such use.
entries.note: The universal exclusion of mission-critical work creates a strong, testable commitment.

entries.test: Published analyses and controlled experiments would show whether probabilistic answer generation inherently produces the asserted hallucination behavior.
entries.note: 'Know nothing' is loose language, but the passage offers a testable mechanism for hallucinations.
'Unsustainable' could mean economic, environmental or physical infeasibility, with no specified horizon or limit.
The claim attributes private beliefs and motives to the industry.

entries.test: Public investor presentations, earnings calls and company announcements would show whether big tech predominantly presents generative AI as a source of future growth.
entries.note: The normalized proposition has a plain reading about public investor messaging.
In context, he denies the worth of intermediary services rather than asserting a defined accounting measure.

entries.test: Public evidence of generative AI solving practical problems or earning profits for the named companies by publication would test the categorical denial.
entries.note: Context limits 'AI' to generative AI and distinguishes profits from revenue. The normalization leaves both distinctions unclear.

entries.test: Public financial reporting covering OpenAI through publication would establish whether it had ever earned a profit and how operating costs compared with licensing and subscription revenue.
entries.note: The introductory 'may make billions' does not hedge the extracted loss claim.

entries.test: Public reporting on SGE's monetization and documented SGE outputs at publication would show whether Google had found a way to monetize it and whether it still hallucinated.
entries.note: 'Cannot make money' is stronger than having failed to find a way at that time.
'Good' supplies no shared outcome criterion. The immediate referent is Venkatachary's appointment, not multiple leaders taking ranking and quality roles.

entries.test: Public opinion trends and surveys of reasons for declining trust would show whether dissatisfaction with AI promotion and internet deterioration drove a backlash against tech.
entries.note: 'As a result' makes this a causal claim, and 'I think' does not by itself turn it into a probability estimate.
